content: Self-harm (SH), which includes intentional self-poisoning or self-injury regardless of suicidal intent or other motivations, is an increasingly prevalent issue worldwide. It is often a repetitive behavior and is strongly associated with an elevated risk of suicide. Despite the growing concern, there is a lack of robust evidence regarding the effectiveness of interventions specifically designed for children and adolescents who engage in SH. This is in contrast to the more substantial body of evidence available for psychosocial interventions in adults. To address this gap, this review updates a previous Cochrane Review from 2015, focusing on the role of interventions for SH in individuals under 18 years of age. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of psychosocial interventions, pharmacological agents, or natural products on SH in children and adolescents. These interventions were compared to various types of care, including treatment-as-usual (TAU), routine psychiatric care, enhanced usual care (EUC), active comparators, placebo, alternative pharmacological treatments, or combinations of these. The primary outcome of interest was the recurrence of SH episodes within a maximum follow-up period of two years. Secondary outcomes included treatment adherence, levels of depression, feelings of hopelessness, general and social functioning, suicidal ideation, and completed suicide. The review involved a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Common Mental Disorders Specialized Register, the Cochrane Library, MEDLINE, Embase, and PsycINFO, up to July 4, 2020. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were included if they compared specific psychosocial or pharmacological interventions with the aforementioned types of care in children and adolescents who had experienced a recent SH episode (within six months of trial entry) that required hospital or clinical attention. A total of 17 trials involving 2,280 participants were included in the review. The majority of participants were female (87.6%), with a mean age of 14.7 years (standard deviation 1.5 years). The trials primarily investigated the effectiveness of various psychosocial interventions, as none of the included studies evaluated pharmacological agents in this population. Dialectical behavior therapy for adolescents (DBT-A) was associated with a lower rate of SH repetition (30%) compared to TAU, EUC, or alternative psychotherapy (43%) at post-intervention. This finding was based on high-certainty evidence from four trials (odds ratio [OR] 0.46, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.26 to 0.82; N = 270). However, for individual cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT)-based psychotherapy, there was no clear evidence of a difference in SH repetition compared to TAU (OR 0.93, 95% CI 0.12 to 7.24; N = 51; low-certainty evidence). Similarly, the effectiveness of mentalization-based therapy for adolescents (MBT-A) in reducing SH repetition compared to TAU was uncertain (OR 0.70, 95% CI 0.06 to 8.46; N = 85; very low-certainty evidence), with substantial heterogeneity observed (I² = 68%). Family therapy showed no evidence of a difference in SH repetition rates compared to TAU or EUC (OR 1.00, 95% CI 0.49 to 2.07; N = 191; moderate-certainty evidence). Additionally, there was no evidence of a difference in SH repetition for compliance enhancement approaches at six months, group-based psychotherapy at six or 12 months, remote contact interventions (e.g., emergency cards) at 12 months, or therapeutic assessment at 12 or 24 months. The authors concluded that the evidence for psychosocial interventions in children and adolescents who engage in SH is limited and of moderate to very low quality. The small number of trials and the variability in findings contribute to the uncertainty. Further research is needed to evaluate the effectiveness of DBT-A, given its promising results. Additionally, individual CBT-based psychotherapy, which has shown benefits in adults who engage in SH, should be further developed and rigorously tested in younger populations.
